title: Return on Equity (ROE)
summary: ROE measures how efficiently a company generates profit from shareholder equity.
content: Return on Equity is calculated as net income divided by average shareholder equity. A higher ROE can indicate efficient use of capital, but it should be interpreted with debt levels, industry norms, and accounting quality. High leverage can inflate ROE, so ROE should not be used alone.

title: Return on Capital Employed (ROCE)
summary: ROCE measures operating profit generated from total capital employed.
content: Return on Capital Employed compares operating profit with the capital used in the business. It is useful for capital-intensive sectors because it considers both equity and debt-funded capital. ROCE should be compared with peers and the company's cost of capital.

title: Price to Earnings Ratio (P/E)
summary: P/E compares a company's share price with its earnings per share.
content: The price to earnings ratio is calculated as market price per share divided by earnings per share. A high P/E may reflect growth expectations or overvaluation, while a low P/E may indicate undervaluation or business risk. It should be interpreted with growth, margins, return ratios, and sector context.

title: Debt to Equity Ratio
summary: Debt to equity compares borrowings with shareholder equity.
content: Debt to equity helps assess financial leverage. A high ratio can increase financial risk because interest and repayment obligations may pressure cash flows. The acceptable level varies by sector; banks and financial companies require different interpretation from manufacturing or technology companies.

title: Free Cash Flow
summary: Free cash flow is cash left after operating expenses and capital expenditure.
content: Free cash flow indicates how much cash a business can generate after maintaining or expanding its asset base. Positive and consistent free cash flow can support dividends, debt reduction, acquisitions, and reinvestment. It should be checked alongside profit quality and working capital trends.

title: Dividend Yield
summary: Dividend yield compares annual dividend with current market price.
content: Dividend yield is calculated as annual dividend per share divided by current share price. A high yield may appeal to income-focused investors, but it can also signal weak price performance or an unsustainable payout. Dividend consistency and cash flow coverage matter.

title: Operating Margin
summary: Operating margin measures operating profit as a percentage of revenue.
content: Operating margin shows how much profit a company earns from core operations before interest and tax. Higher margins may indicate pricing power, cost control, or scale advantages. Margins should be compared with industry peers and historical trends.

title: Market Capitalization
summary: Market capitalization is the total market value of a company's equity.
content: Market capitalization is calculated as current share price multiplied by shares outstanding. It indicates company size in the market, but it is not the same as business quality or intrinsic value. Market cap should be considered with earnings, cash flows, debt, and growth.
